summary: Ganelon's betrayal, Roland's proud last stand at Roncevaux beside Oliver, Charlemagne's grief and vengeance on the Saracens, and the traitor's trial.

hunger.why: Food is never sought or lacking; feasts are not part of the action.

thirst.why: No character seeks or lacks water.

feeling-cold-hot.why: A great storm and darkness over France portend Roland's death, but temperature extremes are not a hardship.

sleepiness.why: Charlemagne's prophetic dreams come in troubled sleep, and the Franks are weary after battle, but fatigue is marginal.

curiosity.why: The Franks campaign through Spain and the Pyrenean passes, but exploring unfamiliar places is not a motive.

explanation-seeking.why: Charlemagne's dreams of bears and leopards foreshadow events, and the trial establishes Ganelon's guilt, but no mystery is investigated.

skill-acquisition.why: Warriors display mastery of sword and lance, but no one trains or improves.

play.why: The opening shows the Frankish knights at chess and backgammon in the orchard at Cordres.

resource-accumulation.why: Marsile buys Ganelon with gold, offers Charlemagne treasure and tribute, and Saragossa is plundered at the end.

resource-foraging.why: No one searches for scarce resources.

mental-time-travel.why: Ganelon plots the ambush with Marsile, Charlemagne's dreams foretell disaster, and Oliver foresees the rearguard's doom.

fear-of-predators.why: Bears, leopards, and a boar threaten Charlemagne only in dreams; animals are symbols, not dangers.

fear-of-aggressors.why: The ambush at Roncevaux, wave after wave of Saracen attack, and the battle with Baligant's host fill the poem.

fear-of-heights.why: The high Pyrenean passes are named, but no fall or vertigo threatens anyone.

disgust.why: The field is strewn with corpses and Marsile loses his hand, but contamination is not dwelt on.

pain-aversion.why: Oliver's brains run from his skull, Roland's temples burst from blowing the horn, and Ganelon is torn apart by horses.

pride.why: Roland lives for renown and will not have shameful songs sung of him; his feats and Charlemagne's glory define the poem.

shame.why: Roland refuses to sound the horn because it would shame him and his lineage, and Oliver later reproaches his recklessness.

moral-pride.why: Roland, Oliver, and Turpin fight to the death for Charlemagne and Christendom: Christians are right, pagans are wrong.

guilt.why: Roland laments that his pride cost Oliver and the peers their lives, and Ganelon's conscience is briefly troubled.

warmth.why: Roland tenderly lays out his dead companions and embraces the dying Oliver, and Charlemagne cherishes Roland.

moral-blame.why: Ganelon's treason is condemned by Roland, Charlemagne, and the barons; his trial, Pinabel's defeat, and his execution close the poem.

moral-praise.why: Roland dies a martyr, angels carry his soul to heaven, and Charlemagne mourns him as the finest knight.

revenge.why: Ganelon betrays Roland to avenge his nomination, Roland avenges his men, and Charlemagne crushes Marsile and Baligant for Roland.

forgiveness.why: Roland and Oliver reconcile before Oliver dies, and Turpin absolves the doomed rearguard.

compassion.why: Roland weeps over his fallen peers and Charlemagne pities the slain, but protecting the vulnerable is not a theme.

affiliation.why: Ganelon and Marsile swear a treacherous bond, and Bramimonde is received into the Frankish fold by conversion.

friendship.why: Roland and Oliver's companionship, their quarrel, and their deaths side by side are the poem's emotional core.

sadness.why: Charlemagne faints with grief over Roland, Roland mourns Oliver, and Aude falls dead at the news.

humor.why: Beyond grim boasts there is no comedy.

embarrassment.why: Ganelon is humiliated when Roland laughs at his nomination as envoy.

reasoning.why: Councils debate Marsile's offer, Roland and Oliver argue over the horn, and Ganelon's trial turns on competing pleas.

coalitional-affiliation.why: Franks against Saracens, Christendom against paganism, and the twelve peers as a sworn band define every allegiance.

status-seeking.why: Roland's standing as Charlemagne's champion, the honor of leading the rearguard, and Baligant's claim to supremacy drive the conflict.

envy.why: Ganelon resents Roland's favor with Charlemagne and his prominence among the peers.

anger.why: Ganelon's rage at Roland sets the plot in motion, and Charlemagne's wrath drives the war of vengeance.

hatred.why: Ganelon relishes Roland's doom, pagans and Christians exult over each other's dead, and Charlemagne wants Ganelon destroyed.

romantic-affiliation.why: Aude is betrothed to Roland and Bramimonde is Marsile's queen, but no courtship is shown.

sexual-attraction.why: Bramimonde's beauty is noted in passing; desire plays no role.

long-term-love.why: Aude's devotion to Roland is so complete that she dies when she hears of his death.

sexual-jealousy.why: No sexual rivalry or infidelity appears.

sexual-disgust.why: No inappropriate or forced sexual relations appear.

parental-care.why: Charlemagne acts as a protective father to his nephew Roland, and Marsile loses his son in battle.

parental-investment.why: Charlemagne is said to have raised Roland, but nurturing is not shown.

familial-love.why: Charlemagne's love for his nephew, Ganelon's hostility to his stepson, and Pinabel's defense of his kinsman make kinship central.
